courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice
md: 3DGS trades memory for speed: hundreds of megabytes of explicit parameters instead of a few megabytes of network weights, in exchange for rendering at well over 30 FPS and training in tens of minutes.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Removing a stage is not always a clean subtraction. You must decide what replaces it: no rewrite at all, or a trivial rewrite; BM25 alone, or BM25 with more candidates to keep the reranker's input size equal. State the replacement, because different choices give different deltas.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: IDOR and BOLA: changing one number in the URL
md: The OWASP API Security Top 10 warns that comparing the session's user id with an id parameter covers only a small subset of BOLA cases. Objects are often shared (a team folder, a manager viewing a report), so the real question is "may this user perform this action on this object under our policy", which lessons 11 and 12 turn into one reusable check.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Enforce authorization in one place: deny by default, policy engines
md: Central does not mean single. Next.js apps that checked access only in middleware were exposed when CVE-2025-29927 let requests skip middleware (lesson 7). Decide policy in one place, but enforce it at more than one layer: at the route, and again at the data (scoped queries, RLS).

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Moving a service account to AES is not a fix by itself. An AES ticket for `Summer2019!` is still crackable; it only costs more per guess. The fix is a password nobody can guess: a gMSA or a long random secret.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AD CS: when a certificate template hands out admin
md: In AD a certificate trusted for client authentication is a password that survives password resets. ESC1 is a template that lets any user choose the name in the certificate. Audit templates, treat CAs as Tier 0, watch 4886 and 4887 for mismatched subjects, and revoke rather than reset.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: OOXML: a zip of XML parts, and links that fetch remote content
md: A document can be dangerous with zero bytes of code inside it. In OOXML, read every .rels part: one line with TargetMode External can be the whole attack.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Anti-debugging and anti-VM: recognising checks and getting past them
md: An empty sandbox report means 'not observed in this environment', never 'benign'. Say exactly that in your notes and in any verdict you hand to the SOC.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Format string bugs as read and write primitives
md: A format string bug is a primitive factory: the read directives leak, and %n writes. The cure is structural and cheap: constant format strings, enforced by -Werror=format-security and static analysis.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Black-box attacks: transfer, substitutes and query access
md: Keeping weights secret is not a defence against evasion. Transfer means an attacker can rehearse on their own copy and arrive with inputs that already work. Secrecy raises the cost; it is never the control.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Membership inference: was this record in the training set?
md: "The model is only exposed through an API, so the training data is safe" is false. Query access is all membership inference needs (NIST's capability list). Report TPR at low FPR, not just average accuracy, when you audit.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Command and control at the design level
md: Do not treat C2 detection as "find the red team's tool". CISA's federal red team (AA24-193A) "deployed over seven different implants" with different host and network signatures precisely to show that defenders who hunt one framework's fingerprints miss the rest. Detect the behaviour every implant shares: periodic contact, new destinations, odd egress from servers.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Reporting, retesting and where to practise
md: Measure a red or purple team by what it changes: findings with owners, fixes retested with the same procedure, and tests that keep running afterwards. Everything is done under written authorisation, inside agreed rules, with a way to stop in minutes.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: The model does not execute tools. It only emits a structured request. Whether a shell command actually runs, and with what permissions, is decided entirely by harness code, which is why safety controls belong in the harness.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The read path: scoring memories by recency, importance and relevance
md: Recency decay does not resolve conflicts. A stale fact with high importance and relevance still makes the cut, so the newer fact helps only if the reader happens to trust it more. Resolve contradictions on the write path; use scoring to choose among facts that are all still true.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
md: An agentic RL environment is a benchmark task turned into a loop you can run millions of times: `reset` to a clean sandbox, `step` per tool call, and a programmatic checker that produces the reward at the end. The simulated user in tau-bench is part of the environment, not part of the policy.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: A toy agent loop: watching a web page give orders
md: The dangerous line is never the model call. It is the loop that turns model output into actions. Put your controls there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Model supply chain: pickle files, safetensors and signing
md: Loading a pickle is running code. Prefer safetensors, load PyTorch files with weights_only=True, and verify a signature or hash from a source you trust before loading anything.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Cheap surrogates for DFT: graph networks and interatomic potentials
md: Judge a discovery surrogate by what it does to DFT spending: precision (hit rate), recall, and DAF on unrelaxed inputs. A low regression error does not guarantee good decisions near the hull.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a green-list watermark and detector in 60 lines
md: The two p-values for the watermarked run differ by a factor of about 78,000 ($5.9 \times 10^{-30}$ versus $4.6 \times 10^{-25}$). Both are tiny here, but the same gap at a borderline score decides whether someone is accused. Three Bricks reports exact tests because the normal tail is too optimistic exactly where thresholds sit, deep in the tail.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
md: What interposition misses: statically linked programs (LD_PRELOAD is a feature of the dynamic linker), secure-execution binaries such as set-user-ID programs (the linker ignores LD_PRELOAD paths with slashes), and any memory that bypasses malloc: direct mmap, custom arenas and pools, GPU allocations. heaptrack's README notes pool allocators need code annotations to be profiled.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: LOF answers a different question from Isolation Forest: not how isolated a point is, but how isolated it is relative to its own neighborhood. Use it when normal data has regions of very different density; pay for it with k-nearest-neighbor searches and a k to tune.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), item by item
md: Most of the API Top 10 is not exotic. It is a missing check (who owns this, who may call this, how many times), a forgotten endpoint, or misplaced trust in another system.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OpenID Connect: logging users in with an ID token
md: ID token: for the client, proves a login happened (check aud = your client_id and nonce). Access token: for the API, grants access (the API checks aud = itself). Never accept one where the other is expected.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to API and token attacks
md: Tokens move the security perimeter into data: who issued it, with which key, for which audience, for how long. Log those fields on every request, alert on the impossible ones, and rehearse revoking at scale.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Writing rules: Semgrep and CodeQL on the same code
md: Write a custom rule when a bug teaches you a pattern: after every incident or review finding, ask "where else does this pattern appear?" and encode it. That is variant analysis, and it turns one fix into a class fix.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: SSVC: decisions instead of scores
md: SSVC turns "how bad is it?" into "what do we do, and how fast?". The inputs that matter most are exploitation status and your own context: exposure and how essential the system is. A score cannot know the second.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
md: ARIES in one line: **repeat history, then undo the losers, logging every undo as a redo-only CLR whose UndoNextLSN skips what is already undone**. That makes recovery **idempotent**, meaning that running it again after a partial run ends in the same state as running it once: crash during analysis or redo and you simply start over; crash during undo and you resume where the CLRs say.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
md: `gather` does not cancel siblings on failure. With the default `return_exceptions=False`, the first exception propagates to the caller but the docs state the other awaitables "won't be cancelled and will continue to run". If you want per-item errors without losing the batch, pass `return_exceptions=True` and inspect each result; if one failure should stop everything, use a `TaskGroup`.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: The budget only helps tasks that keep awaiting **Tokio** resources. It cannot interrupt a tight CPU loop or a blocking call, and the Tokio team has said it will not detect blocked workers and add threads automatically. Fixing those is your job.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: A pretrained audio model never sees a whole clip at once. It sees fixed 0.96 s log-mel patches and returns one embedding and one score vector per patch. Everything about clip-level decisions (lesson 3) is about combining those per-patch outputs.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: How offline cracking works: guesses, lists, rules and arithmetic
md: Offline cracking = guess, hash, compare, at the attacker's full hardware speed. Defenders control two things: how many guesses a password needs (length, unpredictability, blocklists) and how expensive each guess is (a slow, salted hash).

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Wearing MFA down: SIM swaps, push fatigue and Uber 2022
md: MFA is only as strong as its weakest step. SMS inherits the phone network's weaknesses; plain push inherits human fatigue. Number matching helps against fatigue; phishing-resistant MFA removes the whole class.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: End-to-end science agents: AI Scientist and co-scientist
md: End-to-end science agents fail at the steps where nothing external checks them: invented numbers, unfair comparisons, edits to their own limits. Put independent checks (sandboxes, reproducibility, human experts) at exactly those points.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: x86-64 on Linux and macOS: the System V calling convention
md: Do not apply Windows habits to Linux binaries. On Windows the first argument is in `rcx`; on Linux and macOS `rcx` is the fourth. Misreading the convention shifts every argument by several positions and makes a correct analysis look nonsensical. Check the file format first: PE means Microsoft x64, ELF or Mach-O on x86-64 means System V.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Ternary weights: log2(3), absmean and the power of zero
md: "1-bit LLM" is the family name, not the bit count. BitNet b1.58 weights are ternary (about 1.58 bits), the original BitNet was binary (1 bit), and in both the activations are 8-bit and the embeddings stay in higher precision.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a tiny BitNet and run it from packed bytes
md: The whole method fits on a laptop: a quantizer in the forward pass, an STE in the backward pass, then 2 bits per weight and integer adds at inference. The hard part in practice is the kernel, and matching training's quantizers exactly.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: A browser runs hostile code all day: the threat model
md: Misconception: "a sandbox escape is worse than a renderer bug, so it must be Critical." Chromium rates a renderer sandbox escape **High** because it needs the precondition of a compromised renderer. Critical is reserved for bugs that reach privileged code straight from a web page, or full chains.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Memory safety strategy: the Rule of 2, MiraclePtr, Rust and RLBox
md: Misconception: "a sandbox makes a memory bug harmless." It makes it worth less. A sandboxed decoder bug still gives code execution inside that sandbox, which is why Chromium still fixes and rewards such bugs as High, and why the Rule of 2 prefers removing the unsafe language when it can.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Compaction: merging sorted runs and organizing levels
md: Compaction converts a growing pile of overlapping files into a few large sorted runs. It is what keeps LSM reads and space bounded, and it is paid for with extra writes: every byte is rewritten each time it moves down a level.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU-K: evict by the K-th most recent reference
md: LRU-K is not "keep the last K timestamps and you are done". Without a correlated reference period, a transaction that touches a page twice in a millisecond makes it look hot; without retained history, every page re-entering the pool starts at infinite distance and is evicted first.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Availability engineering: nines, redundancy and failure domains
md: Availability = uptime over total time. Hard dependencies multiply availabilities; independent redundant copies multiply failure rates; MTTR is a lever as strong as MTBF. Redundancy is only as good as its independence, so map failure domains, including software versions and admin identities.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups attackers cannot reach: immutability and isolated recovery
md: Assume production identity is lost. Give backups their own control plane, immutable and time-based retention, delayed and out-of-band-approved deletions, keys you cannot lose, alerts on every significant change, and restore into an isolated environment before anything returns to production.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Regulated resilience: DORA testing, TLPT and UK impact tolerances
md: DORA requires a BIA, backup and restore procedures with segregated restore systems, yearly continuity and switchover tests, a crisis function, and TLPT on production every three years for designated firms. The UK sets impact tolerances per important business service and requires proof, by severe but plausible scenario tests, that firms stay within them.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Generating with patches: the BLT decoding loop and its real cost
md: In BLT generation the latent model runs only when a patch closes, but the entropy model, encoder and decoder run on every byte in sequence. Fewer FLOPs per byte and lower latency are different goals; fixed patches, caches and speculative drafting are the levers for the second.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Data races: pthreads in C versus Send and Sync in Rust
md: Data race: unsynchronized conflicting accesses, undefined behavior, ruled out at compile time by the borrow rules plus Send and Sync. Race condition: a timing-dependent logic bug, still possible, still memory safe.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Why one load can cost 3 cycles or 240
md: Latency numbers are not constants of nature. Drepper's are for a Pentium M, CMU's for Haswell, and every CPU differs. Use them to reason about *ratios* (a DRAM access costs tens to hundreds of L1 hits), and measure your own machine before quoting absolute cycles.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Activation patching worked through: two directions and a shortcut
md: Denoising asks whether a component is enough to restore the behavior; noising asks whether the behavior needs it. AND-like circuits hide from denoising, OR-like backups hide from noising, and gradient shortcuts are trustworthy only for small patches.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
md: An attribution graph explains one prompt in one replacement model. It is not proof of a general algorithm, it is silent about attention's choices, and any path through error nodes is unexplained. State those limits whenever you report a circuit.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: Pick the propensity source by how much user disruption you can afford: randomization or swaps are simplest and most trustworthy, EM and intervention harvesting use existing logs but rest on model assumptions, and DLA learns everything jointly. Every option inherits the click model's assumptions; if users behave like a cascade, a position-only propensity is misspecified.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Browser extensions: someone else's code in every page
md: Nothing on facebook.com was vulnerable in that case. An extension with access to a site is effectively a trusted script on that site. For a site owner this risk sits outside your perimeter; for an organisation that manages its employees' browsers, it is squarely inside it.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Where the evidence lives when there is no server to seize
md: Cloud incident response reconstructs what identities did through the provider's API, across four evidence layers: control plane, data plane, workload and identity provider. What you can prove is decided before the incident, by which logs were on and where they were kept.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Identity incidents: tokens, consent grants and mailbox rules
md: Misconception: "we reset the password, so the attacker is out". A reset leaves forwarding rules, registered MFA methods, OAuth consent grants and app passwords in place, and already issued access tokens keep working for up to about an hour in apps without CAE. Disable, revoke, then hunt for each kind of persistence.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: The same guardrails in Azure Policy and Google organization policy
md: Identity rules (RBAC, IAM) say who may act. Configuration guardrails (Azure Policy, Google organization policy, AWS SCPs used as preventive controls) say what no one may build, such as storage that accepts account keys or service accounts with downloadable keys. Set them high in the hierarchy, start in audit mode, then deny.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The shared responsibility model, and when the provider gets it wrong
md: Common misconception: "we are on a big cloud, so the provider handles security." The provider secures its platform. Your identities, keys, data and configuration are yours, and even provider-side bugs usually ended with a customer to-do: regenerate keys after ChaosDB, update agents after OMIGOD.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Logging and detection: what key abuse looks like in CloudTrail
md: Log everything that changes configuration, keep it in a place attackers cannot reach, turn on data events for buckets that hold sensitive data, and alert on a short list of high-signal events: logging disabled, root use, new access keys and users, policy changes, and known credentials used from new places.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Three things the silhouette cannot do. It is undefined for k = 1, so it can never tell you "this data has no clusters" (our k = 3 winner at 0.54 is not strong evidence of anything). It needs all pairwise distances, so it costs O(n squared) work. And it rewards compact well-separated blobs, so it is biased toward the kind of answer k-means produces, which makes it a poor referee between k-means and a density method.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: A column in memory is a few flat buffers: values (or offsets plus data) and a validity bitmap. Flat, typed, contiguous buffers are what make tight loops and SIMD over columns possible.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Misconception: the `inline` keyword forces inlining. It is a hint plus linkage rules: rules about how the function's definition is shared between files. At -O2 the compiler inlines functions you never marked, and may refuse ones you did. At -O0 GCC inlines nothing unless the function has `__attribute__((always_inline))`.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: -ffast-math assumes no NaNs or infinities (-ffinite-math-only), so code that relies on IEEE behavior of NaNs and infinities can give incorrect results. Clang has deprecated -Ofast because an optimization flag changing the observable behavior of correct code surprises people. Enable fast-math per file or per function when you have verified the numerics, not globally.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Misconception: a system prompt saying "ignore instructions on web pages" solves injection. It helps, but the model reads that prompt and the attacker's text through the same channel. Defenses that do not depend on the model obeying (no secrets in the VM, network allowlists, harness-enforced confirmations) are what hold when the model is fooled.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: TSan must see **all** synchronization. Code not built with the flag (a prebuilt library, inline assembly) can cause false positives or missed races. That is why Rust's std should be rebuilt with the sanitizer via `-Zbuild-std`. The Rust unstable book also says Rust TSan does not support `std::sync::atomic::fence` or synchronization done in inline assembly, and rebuilding std does not change that.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
md: Herlihy and Wing showed sequential consistency is **not local**: every object can be sequentially consistent while the system as a whole is not. Linearizability is local, which is one reason it composes better.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Must-haves and nice-to-haves need different machinery
md: Hard constraints decide **who is in**; soft constraints decide **the order**. Never let a preference buy its way past a requirement, and never let a preference silently remove someone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: SAT solvers: DPLL, unit propagation and clause learning
md: CDCL = DPLL + conflict analysis that learns a clause + backjumping to the level where the learned clause becomes unit and forces (asserts) its last literal + watched literals for cheap propagation + activity-based decisions and restarts. Each conflict teaches the solver something it never has to rediscover.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
md: Pin by digest so you always run the same bytes; sign in CI and verify at admission so you only run bytes your pipeline produced.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
md: A pod's identity is its service account token plus whatever cloud role it can reach. Mount tokens only where needed, give each app its own service account, and map cloud access per service account instead of per node.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Escapes in the runtime: runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels
md: Runtime escapes come from the runtime briefly holding host resources while entering a container. Patch the runtime everywhere, run only trusted images, and use user namespaces so that even a successful escape lands as an unprivileged user.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Deletes and resets are rare in training data and rare in casual testing, so they are the operations most likely to be broken in your system. Test them on purpose: write cases for *drop X*, *any X is fine*, *never mind the Y* and *start over*.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Storing state server-side and measuring it
md: Store the state server-side with a version and an event log; evaluate it with joint goal accuracy and per-operation recall, not just slot accuracy or end-to-end clicks.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Unfaithful without a hint: rationalization on natural prompts
md: Reversed question pairs detect unfaithfulness without planting anything: a consistent reasoner cannot answer Yes to both. This is behavioral evidence, necessary but not sufficient for faithful internal computation, and it shows frontier models rationalize rarely but measurably.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
md: Three independent facts, often confused. A stream gives you **ordering** (and is always sequential inside itself). Separate streams give you **permission** to overlap. The hardware (`asyncEngineCount`, concurrent kernel support, free SMs) decides whether overlap actually **happens**. Two streams on a one-copy-engine GPU will still serialize their two transfers against each other.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: Joint attention makes each document token's representation a function of the query. That is the source of the accuracy gain and the reason nothing beyond tokenization can be reused across queries.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
md: Any cipher that XORs a keystream onto data must never produce the same keystream twice. Remember this; it returns in lessons 6, 7 and 15 under the names counter reuse, nonce reuse and ECDSA nonce reuse.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
md: Most cryptographic failures in the wild are not broken maths. They are reused nonces, weak randomness, unchecked parameters, outdated algorithms and home-made constructions. Security review of crypto code is mostly checking these nine rules.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Secret-dependent timing: comparisons, Minerva and TPM-Fail
md: Any secret that influences control flow, memory addresses or loop lengths can leak through time, over a network or from another process. Use library functions built to be constant time, keep crypto libraries and firmware patched, and never write your own comparison or scalar multiplication.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
md: A layout is just a function: coordinate in, integer offset out, computed as an inner product with the strides. Everything else in CuTe (tiling, partitioning across threads, MMA operand maps) is built by combining such functions.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
md: CXL attacks two problems at once: capacity and bandwidth that DDR pins cannot scale (memory *expansion*), and DRAM that is stuck on the wrong host (memory *pooling*). Both rely on one property: the CPU reaches the memory with plain loads and stores, so applications do not change.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
md: Ask three questions every time: is it legal (law), is it authorised (the owner, in writing, in scope), is it right (harm to others). Keep evidence of each answer before you start.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Crossing borders: the Budapest Convention and jurisdiction
md: Testing a system abroad from home does not put you under only your own country's law. Both CMA section 5 and CyBOK's analysis point the same way: the target's location can be enough.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Monitoring, interception and privacy law in security work
md: Login banners are not magic. They support consent and notice, but they do not authorise intercepting people who never saw them (a visitor on guest Wi-Fi, the other party to an email), and they do not override necessity and retention limits.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a researcher's decision checklist
md: Every lesson's cases share one pattern: the person in trouble had a story that made sense to them ('it was public', 'they agreed afterwards', 'it's only code', 'nothing was merged'). The checklist exists because your own story is the hardest one to see past.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Mixtures that change during training: annealing data and mid-training
md: A gain from an anneal is not proof that the data would help as much over a full pretraining run, or at a larger scale. Llama 3's math annealing helped the 8B model a lot and the 405B model hardly at all. Use anneals to rank candidate datasets, then confirm at the scale you care about.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
md: Vectorizing the instructions does not fix the layout. Vectorizing means rewriting a scalar loop, which handles one element per instruction, into SIMD instructions that handle 8 at once, and compilers can do it automatically. Even if a compiler vectorizes an AoS loop, the x values are still 12 bytes apart, so each register still needs a gather and the loop still pays for every unused byte in each line.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds
md: Collect only what the purpose needs, give every record type a retention period and a trigger, enforce it with a job (not a policy document), and make legal holds the only thing that stops the job.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Insider risk: definitions, the Tesla files and running a programme
md: Insiders already have access, so the programme rests on context (HR events, role), behaviour against the person's own baseline, and exfiltration routes, combined as sequences. Build it with HR, legal and privacy from the start, and pseudonymise until there is cause.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honeytokens and canary tokens: data that phones home
md: A hosted token service sees your alerts: the alert, including the triggering address, goes to whoever runs the token server. For sensitive placements, run your own. Thinkst publishes the Canarytokens server as open source and recommends its Docker image for self-hosting.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
md: Floating-point addition is commutative but not associative. Reordering a sum is not a refactor, it is a different computation. Every other idea in this course follows from that sentence.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
md: To find rare bugs, maximize the *diversity* of runs, not the intensity of each one. Random per-run choices of faults, features and buggify sites cover far more distinct states than one heavily tuned configuration.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Reviewing infrastructure as code: reading a Terraform plan
md: The most dangerous line in a plan is often not an open port but a `-/+` or `-` on something stateful: a database, a bucket, a KMS key. Replacements are triggered by innocent-looking edits (a renamed resource, a changed engine version), and a reviewer skimming for security groups will miss them.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Build it: turn your GPT into a masked diffusion LM
md: Three edits turn a GPT into a masked diffusion LM: a [MASK] id, `is_causal=False`, and targets at the same positions as the inputs. In practice add a fourth, relative positions such as RoPE, so the bidirectional model learns locality quickly. At equal size and steps it trains to a worse likelihood than the GPT, and its samples get better as each pass commits fewer tokens.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput = the highest rate at which at least 90% (or your target) of requests meet every latency SLO, divided by the GPUs used. It is the number disaggregation is designed to raise.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Disaggregation at scale: MoE, expert parallelism and elastic pools
md: Scaling or admitting on the current load of the other pool oscillates. Mooncake saw it with early rejection: decode looks idle, so many requests are admitted; they reach decode one prefill later, decode looks full, so admissions stop and prefill idles, and the cycle repeats in opposite phase. Its fix was to decide on the decode load predicted for when the request will arrive there.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
md: These artefacts show that a *user account* interacted with a file, a folder or a drive. They are strongest together and with the drive in hand.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
md: Beam width W trades round trips for wasted reads; search list L trades reads for recall. Tune L for the recall target first, then pick the smallest W that meets the latency target, watching total reads against the SSD's IOPS budget.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: Turning a pair into one desirable and one undesirable example, as the paper does to compare against DPO, is described by its authors as a naive assumption: a chosen answer is only better than its sibling, not necessarily good.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Not every mismatch is a bug in the new store. If the new store is fed asynchronously, from a queue or a CDC stream, it is eventually consistent with the old one: a read right after a write can compare a fresh control with a candidate that is milliseconds behind. Measure that lag, and only `ignore` such cases after confirming they converge.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: X3DH's fine print: signed prekeys, replay, deniability, misbinding
md: Verify every signature on a bundle before any DH, abort on failure, delete one-time prekey private keys after use, rotate signed prekeys, rate-limit bundle fetches, and make the session's next key depend on fresh randomness from Bob.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Metadata: sealed sender and the statistics that undo it
md: Hiding a field is not hiding a pattern. Any metadata defence must be judged over many messages and against an observer who sees timing, sizes and automatic replies, not one message at a time.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Operational failures: Signalgate and the TeleMessage archive (2025)
md: E2EE protects the channel between ends. It cannot decide who the ends are (group membership), what an end does with plaintext (archiving clients, screenshots, backups), or whether that channel is the right one for the information (classification and records policy).

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Estimate cost as event rate x cost per event. Keep the rate low (stable, specific probes; filters; sampling) and keep the work in the kernel (maps, not printf). That is what makes bpftrace usable on a live production system.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Pulse Secure and FortiOS, 2019: file reads that leaked passwords
md: Patching closes the hole. It does not un-leak what already leaked. After any file-read bug on an edge device, rotate every secret the device held and every password typed through it.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Responding to a compromised appliance: evidence, rebuild, rotate
md: Evidence first, then the fix. Collect what the vendor's procedure allows before patching or rebooting, isolate without powering off once compromise is found, patch, and if compromise is possible rebuild and rotate every secret the device held or saw.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: L1-Exact spends the requested budget even when the problem is easy, because its reward penalizes being too short. When the goal is a worst-case cost cap rather than an exact length, use the Max formulation, which matched or beat L1-Exact while often using up to 2x fewer tokens.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: One input, many readers: where encoding bugs come from
md: Misconception: "the filter should just decode more". A filter in front of an application cannot know how many decoding or normalising steps come later, or in what order. Make the component that acts on the value own the check, and treat upstream filters as an extra layer, not the defence.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Canonical identifiers and idempotence: the Spotify takeover
md: Test canonicalisation functions for idempotence (`f(f(x)) == f(x)`) on every input you accept, and refuse inputs that fail. Store and compare only the canonical form; never re-canonicalise an already-canonical value and expect it to stay put unless that property is enforced.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Defender's checklist for encodings and parsers, and where to practise
md: Two questions catch most bugs in this course: "Is this check running on the exact value that will be used?" and "Is anything else going to parse these bytes?"

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control II: App Control for Business, drivers and LOLBins
md: Allowlisting answers "should this code run at all?", a question EDR never asks. Start in audit, read every 3076, block LOLBins you do not need, keep the driver blocklist on, and then treat every 3077 as a signal.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
md: Event-based NILM reads each step as one appliance switching. When two appliances switch inside one sample, the switch continuity assumption breaks: the net step looks like a third, unrelated appliance, and the ON/OFF bookkeeping fails for both. Higher sample rates make such coincidences rarer but never impossible.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: Each field adds $\log_2(m/u)$. Agreement on a rare value (a domain) is worth far more than agreement on a common one (a city), and a missing field adds nothing instead of counting as a disagreement.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
md: Misconception: deleting a malicious app from Enterprise applications removes it for good. Deleting the service principal removes this tenant's instance; the application object lives in the attacker's tenant, and any user who consents again recreates the service principal. Disable it so it cannot obtain tokens or be consented to.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
md: Misconception: phishing-resistant MFA stops device code phishing. The victim authenticates on the genuine Entra page, so FIDO2 or passkeys work exactly as designed and the tokens still go to whoever started the flow. The fix is to block the flow, not to strengthen the login.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
md: Misconception: the Entra Connect server is 'just a sync box' that a server team can patch and manage like any other. Its connector account can replicate every password hash from AD and its cloud account can write users to the tenant. Microsoft requires treating it as Tier 0.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: Readiness is a hint, not a promise. The [select(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/select.2.html) page warns that a socket can be reported readable and a following read can still block, for example when the arrived packet had a bad checksum and was dropped. That is why event loops always use nonblocking sockets.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
md: Hold out queries, not pairs, and cluster near-duplicates before splitting. Tune on dev as much as you like, read the sealed test set rarely and for decisions you declared in advance, and replace it on a schedule.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Non-executable memory: the NX bit, DEP and W^X
md: NX turns "write code, then run it" into "write data, then crash". It does not stop the hijack of the return address; it removes the attacker's easiest thing to jump *to*.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
md: False sharing needs three things at once: two or more cores, one cache line, and at least one writer. Remove any one (single thread, separate lines, or read-only data) and the line stops bouncing.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Cheaper rounds and smarter servers: compression and FedOpt
md: FedAvg is server SGD with learning rate 1 on the pseudo-gradient $-\Delta_t$. A server optimizer changes how fast and how smoothly the model moves along the averaged client delta. It cannot change where that delta points: the drifted fixed point of lesson 5 is a fixed point for every server optimizer, because there the averaged delta is zero.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma
md: Misconception: "just raise M in HNSW". The paper notes that Qdrant's earlier densification idea did this, but $M$ also sets HNSW's level multiplier $m_L = 1/\ln M$, so raising it flattens the hierarchy, and HNSW is sensitive to its number of levels. ACORN keeps $M$ (and therefore $m_L$ and the level structure) fixed and expands the lists by $\gamma$ instead.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: MoE on real hardware: expert parallelism, all-to-all and serving
md: MoE cost is not just FLOPs. Every layer adds two all-to-alls that must be overlapped with compute, small experts need many tokens per step to stop being memory-bound, and serving must keep all experts resident and batch widely enough that reading their weights is shared by many tokens.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Measured boot: PCRs, extend and what each PCR records
md: Misconception: "The TPM checks the boot." It does not decide anything. It only stores what firmware and loaders tell it. Enforcement comes from Secure Boot, from sealing, or from a remote verifier reading the values (lesson 11).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
md: Misconception: "attention is two GEMMs, so it runs at GEMM speed." The softmax between them is cheap in FLOPs but runs on units hundreds of times slower than the tensor cores. FP8 makes it worse: matmul throughput doubles while exponential throughput stays the same.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: MLA in FlashInfer: attention over a compressed latent cache
md: A classic bug: setting `sm_scale` to $1/\sqrt{576}$ because the kernel's dot products are 576 wide. Absorption only regroups the original product $q^C \cdot k^C + q^R \cdot k^R$, whose head dimension was $128 + 64 = 192$, so the scale stays $1/\sqrt{192}$. FlashInfer's own test comments it as the head dimension before matrix absorption.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLA+ basics: a system is states plus allowed steps
md: A primed equation is not an assignment; an action is a true-or-false formula about a pair of states. If an action says nothing about a variable, the next value is unconstrained. TLC refuses such a spec: dropping `UNCHANGED tmp` from Write makes it stop with "Successor state is not completely specified by action Write".

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus on real data: views, quantifiers, triggers and failed proofs
md: Write quantified specs so that the terms your proof naturally mentions match the triggers. Relate arbitrary pairs (v[i] <= v[j]) rather than neighbors when the code jumps around, and keep nonlinear or bitwise facts in small by(...) queries.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
md: Not every tensor tolerates coarse grouping. DeepSeek tried quantizing activation gradients in 128x128 blocks (so only a transpose would be needed in the backward pass). A 16B MoE model trained for about 300B tokens diverged: Dgrad feeds every earlier layer in a chain and is very precision-sensitive. Activation gradients keep fine 1x128 tiles.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Abuse economics: make every attempt cost more than it earns
md: Profit per attempt is $s\,v - c$. Every control you add should be able to say which of the three it moves, and by how much, and what it costs honest users.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: CAPTCHAs, their limits and privacy-preserving tokens
md: A CAPTCHA is a price, not a wall. Verify it on the server, bind it to the action, make it single use, show it only when risk is high, and watch its solve rate for signs it has been broken.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card testing, 3-D Secure and strong customer authentication
md: Card testing costs you even when every attempt is declined. Protect every endpoint that can touch a card with server-verified challenges and shaped rate limits, and use 3-D Secure to move risky card-not-present payments onto the issuer's authentication.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake reviews and content abuse
md: Inauthentic content shows as copies and groups: near-duplicate text, bursts, and lockstep reviewer sets. Known harmful media is matched with perceptual hashes against shared lists, never by collecting it yourself.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Trading latency for throughput: commit_delay and async commit
md: `synchronous_commit = off` and `fsync = off` sound similar but are not. The first may lose the last ~600 ms (by default) of acknowledged commits and stays consistent. The second can corrupt the whole cluster (PostgreSQL's word for all the databases one server manages) and is only for data you can recreate, such as an initial bulk load.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
md: "Unique crashes" is not a bug count. When a tool, a vendor pitch or your own dashboard reports it, ask how deduplication was done and how many distinct fixes the crashes needed.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery: what is verified so far
md: Verified so far: AI agents can find real bugs by variant analysis (Big Sleep, SQLite), AI-written harnesses extend fuzzing coverage and find real CVEs (OSS-Fuzz, OpenSSL), and attackers use AI to find logic flaws (GTIG 2026). In every defensive case, a concrete reproducer and a sanitizer or test confirmed the bug.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
md: Lucene's javadoc documents a surprise: `FuzzyQuery` on `abcd` with `maxEdits=2` does not match the indexed term `ab`, even though the Levenshtein distance is 2. Engines add rules of their own on top of the textbook distance, so test short terms and other edge cases directly.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
md: A match is not the end product. The solver turns matched star pairs into CRPIX, CRVAL and a CD matrix under a TAN projection, which any FITS tool can then use to label every pixel with RA and Dec.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row
md: A common misconception is that interpolation conventions only matter for image quality. They also move geometry. If training resized with half-pixel centers and inference resizes without them, every pixel coordinate the model predicts is offset by $(s-1)/2$ source pixels, and no amount of retraining the head (the final prediction layers) fixes a preprocessing mismatch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Forgetting record_stream (or calling s0.wait_stream(s1) before the free, which makes all later work on s0 wait for the work already queued on s1) is a silent data race, not a crash: the new tensor's kernel on s0 may overwrite memory that s1 is still reading. The PyTorch docs note the synchronization is needed even when the side stream only writes.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Misalignment, strides and effective bandwidth
md: **Misconception:** the L1 cache makes access patterns irrelevant. Caches help when nearby warps reuse what was over-fetched, as with small misalignments. A large stride over data read once gets no reuse, and every unused byte still crosses the DRAM interface.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Occupancy is a capability, not an achievement. 100 percent occupancy with 5 percent of peak throughput is a latency-bound kernel with plenty of warps and nothing for them to do, and the fix has nothing to do with occupancy.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Occupancy: how many warps fit on an SM at once
md: Higher occupancy is not automatically faster. Low occupancy hurts latency hiding, but past some point extra warps add nothing, and a lower-occupancy kernel can keep more data in registers and avoid spilling (storing values that do not fit in registers out in slower memory). Measure.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: Do not estimate GraphRAG cost from the number of documents alone. Cost scales with total tokens, chunk size, gleaning rounds, the number of entities and relationships that need summaries, and the number of communities. The official docs open with a warning that GraphRAG can consume a lot of LLM resources and suggest starting small.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Build it: GRPO on GSM8K with a small model
md: A reward curve can rise while accuracy does not. If the format reward is easier to earn than the accuracy reward, the summed reward climbs as the model learns the tags, and the accuracy part stays flat. Always log each reward function separately, and evaluate on held-out questions with sampling settings you also use at test time.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Polling, caching and data quality in production
md: A common bug is merging realtime messages instead of replacing state. With FULL_DATASET, a trip missing from the newest message must lose its prediction. Merging keeps stale predictions alive for trips that already finished or were dropped by the producer.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Melissa and ILOVEYOU: viruses that used your address book
md: A blocklist of bad extensions (what the 2000 patch began with) needs constant updating and misses new types. Gateways today block by default and allow a short list of needed types, open documents in protected sandboxes, and Microsoft Office now [blocks macros in files from the internet](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-apps/security/internet-macros-blocked) by default.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Leaks: Snowden, the Shadow Brokers and keeping bugs secret
md: Leaks change risk calculations. Snowden's disclosures pushed internet standards towards encryption by default (RFC 7258). The Shadow Brokers showed that withheld vulnerabilities can escape, which is why governments now publish their rules for disclosure (the VEP charter) and why defenders treat every critical patch as if exploit code will appear soon.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
md: Time profiles answer *where*. Counters answer *why*: low IPC plus many cache misses points at memory, many branch misses points at prediction, high IPC with lots of instructions points at doing too much work.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Power, EM, sound and faults: physical side channels
md: Physical side channels need the attacker close to the device, but that is exactly the threat model of smart cards, phones, payment terminals, hardware wallets and secure enclaves. Hertzbleed shows the line between physical and remote is not fixed: when power controls frequency, power becomes timing.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: What a desync enables, and what defenders see
md: Desync detection is a comparison problem. Log a connection or request identifier at both the front end and the back end, and alert when the request counts or request lines for the same connection differ.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting, responding, and practising safely
md: Desync and cache attacks are the same lesson twice: when two components interpret one message differently, an attacker chooses the difference. Remove ambiguity (HTTP/2 upstream, strict parsing, origin-declared caching), detect disagreement by comparing tiers, and clean up stored state after every fix.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Huge pages are a trade: TLB reach and shorter walks against contiguity, alignment and memory overhead. Use a hugetlbfs pool when you need certainty, THP in madvise mode when the hot regions are known, and check the counters, because both mechanisms fall back silently.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer
md: Choosing a layout: global attention layers buy exact recall at any distance for a growing KV cache; sliding windows cap the cache and cap exact recall with it; shared attention saves parameters, not cache; parallel heads keep a little attention, and a little KV, in every layer. Across these designs the published choices cluster around a small share of global attention, about 1 layer in 4 to 1 in 8, spread evenly.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: A common mistake is to treat a plant like an office network: run an aggressive vulnerability scan, push patches overnight, reboot to clean an infection. NIST warns that indiscriminate use of IT practices in OT 'may cause availability and timing disruptions'. In OT the security team works with control engineers, not around them.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
md: Three layers stood between the change and an overflow: humans watching the HMI (defeated by the replay), network monitoring (raised an alert at minute 10), and an independent safety system with its own sensor (tripped at minute 26). Design so that the last layer does not share any path with the first two.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS
md: Frameworks tell you what good looks like (62443, NIST), what is mandatory in your sector (NERC CIP for the bulk grid), and how attackers behave (ATT&CK for ICS). Use all three, but remember the cases: most real compromises came through remote access, default passwords and flat networks.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: OIDC as the modern alternative: the same job in JSON
md: SAML and OIDC answer the same questions: who issued this, about whom, for which app, for which login, until when, signed with which key. Learn the questions, and either protocol's fields become a checklist.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: The federation defender's checklist, and where to practise
md: Federation turns identity into a few keys and a trust list. Guard those like domain controllers, verify assertions with libraries that use only what was signed, keep sessions short and revocable, and join IdP and app logs so a login that the IdP never issued stands out.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: PAM vaults: check-out, rotation, and the Uber 2022 script
md: A PAM vault turns many secrets into one, rotates them after use, and ideally never shows them to people. That makes the vault and its administrators the most valuable target you own: protect them as the top of the control plane.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu always returns a threshold, even when nothing changed. On a pair with pure noise it will happily split the noise into two classes and flag a large fraction of the image. Check for a clear gap (or a minimum difference between class means) before trusting the mask.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Declaring, severity, the incident commander and the first hour
md: The IC decides and coordinates; they should not also be the person typing commands. When the IC is debugging, nobody is commanding.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Eradication and recovery: rebuild, credentials, krbtgt and backups
md: Replication is not backup. Synchronised copies (domain controllers, mirrored disks, cloud sync) receive the attacker's deletions and encryption as fast as your legitimate changes. Keep at least one copy offline and immutable, and practise restoring it.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
md: Denylist filters ("block quotes, OR, UNION and --") are escaping's weaker cousin. They reject real input such as O'Brien, and they only stop the spellings someone thought of: SQL accepts comments, different case, different whitespace and many equivalent expressions. Lesson 9 shows a real product whose cleaning function was bypassed by finding a path where it was not applied.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows
md: Size the **CQ** for the maximum number of completions that can be outstanding (including several per request for multishot operations, which post many completions from one request, lesson 5), not the SQ. Use `IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE` with `cq_entries`, and reap promptly.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Hands on the chip: fault injection, and code that resists it
md: Hardening raises cost; it does not make a chip invulnerable. The RP2350 errata show two glitches defeating an OTP lock-down (E21) and a glitch that changed which data was signature-checked (E24), both on a chip designed with fault attacks in mind. That is why lesson 8 insists that no unit holds a secret whose loss affects other units.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototypes: where a missing property comes from
md: Reading a missing property silently falls through to the prototype chain, ending at Object.prototype, which nearly every object shares. The keys `__proto__` and `constructor` (then `prototype`) lead from an ordinary object to that shared object. `Object.create(null)` objects have no chain to follow.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Middleware and internal headers: the Next.js bypass
md: Headers that mean something internally (recursion markers, "already authenticated", forwarded client IPs) must either be stripped at the edge or carry proof that only your own infrastructure can produce. And never let one layer be the only authorisation check: Vercel's own advice is not to use middleware as "the sole method of protecting routes".

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
md: Published benchmarks (including those in mimalloc's README and report) measure specific workloads. Allocator rankings change with object sizes, thread counts and cross-thread patterns. Measure throughput, p99 latency (the 99th percentile: the time that 99 percent of requests beat) and RSS (resident set size, the memory actually held in RAM) on your own service, with production-like load, before and after switching.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
md: A common bug is a tuning cache keyed on the kernel name alone, or on batch size only. It never misses, so it never re-tunes, and it silently serves a configuration chosen for a different shape. The symptom is a kernel that is fast in the benchmark that tuned it and mediocre everywhere else.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
md: Measure with the right tool. SPDK reports up to 2.6 times more IOPS per core using its own `perf` example tool than using fio (the Flexible I/O Tester, the standard Linux storage benchmark) with the SPDK plugin for 4 KiB random reads, because fio's flexibility costs cycles. A slow benchmark harness can hide a fast driver.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Case files: BlackByte and Lazarus bring their own drivers
md: The BYOVD timeline runs backwards from what patch management expects: the vendor's fix comes first and the attacks come later. A patch protects machines that run the vendor's software; it does nothing against an attacker who brings the vulnerable version. Only deny rules, by hash or by signer and version, close that gap.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: For memory-bound kernels, runtime is roughly bytes moved / bandwidth. Elementwise ops do so little math per byte that the only lever that matters is how many bytes cross the HBM boundary. Fusion cuts bytes, not FLOPs.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
md: Soft gradient = (q - p) / T, which shrinks like 1 over T squared. Multiply the soft loss by T squared so temperature changes what is matched without changing how much it counts.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: A more accurate teacher is not automatically a better teacher, and a student that improves is not necessarily copying its teacher. Measure student accuracy directly; try a smaller or early-stopped teacher, or a teacher assistant, when the gap is large.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: Rounding error depends on the range of each group. Pre-RoPE keys, per-channel groups, sparse outliers and an FP16 first token all exist to keep group ranges narrow.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
md: Smaller caches only become speed if the attention kernel reads the compressed form directly. Dequantizing to BF16 in a separate pass gives back most of the memory traffic saved.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Capacity offloading: decoding with KV that does not fit in HBM
md: Capacity offloading moves KV every decode step, so it pays only when each crossing is amortized (a big block of sequences sharing each weight load) or shrunk (attention computed where the KV lives, or only the important tokens fetched).

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
md: A smaller wall-clock reading does not mean an event happened before another, and an event that did happen first can carry a larger wall-clock reading, as the last-write-wins example shows. Treat wall time as a hint, never as proof of order.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them
md: Compression is lossy per vector, and the 1-bit setting does cost measurable quality. Treat 2-bit as the safe default and verify 1-bit on your own evaluation set before shipping it.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum
md: The objective never asks a thought to compress the step it replaced. Thoughts are trained only by how much they help predict the remaining steps and the answer, so they are free to become something other than a paraphrase of the text.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: After Coconut: self-distillation, soft thinking, compressed latents
md: Later latent methods differ in what fills the next input slot: a distilled hidden state (CODI), a mixture of token embeddings (Soft Thinking), a sampled compressed embedding (CoLaR) or a discrete code (Token Assorted). Each fixes one of Coconut's limits, and none restores a fully readable trace.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
md: Bigtable's lesson: if you control the layout, make the data follow the model instead of making the model follow the data. Then the prediction is never wrong and there is no last-mile search across blocks.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaRank: weight each pair by what a swap does to NDCG
md: A lambda is a RankNet pair gradient scaled by how much the metric would change if the pair swapped. Pairs that cannot change the top of the list get almost no weight.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Gated DeltaNet: targeted writes plus fast forgetting
md: Gated DeltaNet's one-line change: decay first with a data-dependent $\alpha_t$, then do a delta-rule write with $\beta_t$. $\alpha_t\to0$ clears memory at a context switch; $\alpha_t\to1$ keeps it and lets the delta rule edit single associations.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check
md: Owner, then group, then others: the first class that matches is the only one checked. Write octal as 4 for read, 2 for write, 1 for execute, and remember that umask removes bits from every new file.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo
md: The journal is stored on disk only if `/var/log/journal` exists or journald is configured with `Storage=persistent`. Otherwise it lives in memory under `/run/log/journal` and is lost at reboot (`journald.conf(5)`). Check this before you need the logs, not after an incident.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tailoring, exceptions and rolling a baseline out safely
md: Tailor per host class, waive per host with an owner and an end date, and store both as code so an expired waiver fails on its own. Roll changes out in rings with a scan between rings.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: eBPF: small verified programs that watch the kernel from inside
md: eBPF lets a verified program run at a kernel hook and filter events in the kernel. That makes it the basis of modern Linux sensors. The verifier checks safety, not intent, so treat every BPF program load as a security event.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: Kinsing and TeamTNT, cryptominers on exposed Linux hosts
md: Cryptojacking chains are short and noisy: an exposed service, a root exploit, a service file, a hiding trick, a miner. A hardened, patched baseline breaks the first two steps, and the audit and eBPF rules from this course flag the rest.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Measuring judge agreement: confusion matrix and Cohen's kappa
md: Always say which agreement number you report. UMBRELA's GPT-4o labels on TREC DL 2019 to 2023 had 4-grade kappa 0.31 to 0.37 but binarised kappa 0.42 to 0.50 on the same labels. A paper quoting one and a dashboard quoting the other are not comparable.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Designing human evaluations and measuring agreement
md: Do not report raw percent agreement alone. With skewed labels (say 90% of pairs are ties) two annotators agree often by chance. Report kappa with the confusion matrix, and say how ties were handled.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Measuring a server: latency percentiles, load curves and benchmarks
md: Common benchmarking mistakes: measuring at one rate (or at concurrency 1) and calling it the server's latency; no warm-up; repeated prompts that hit the prefix cache and make TTFT look tiny; output lengths unlike production (too short flatters everything); reporting means without p99; comparing runs with different prompt or output lengths.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Who goes next: priority, fairness and length-aware scheduling
md: Any policy that reorders the queue (SJF, predicted lengths, priority) can starve the requests it keeps pushing back. Production schedulers pair it with an aging rule, a promotion after too many skipped steps, or a fairness counter. And under on-demand allocation a high-priority arrival can trigger preemptions, which cost recomputation (lesson 6).

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: From regex to JSON Schema: grammars, stacks and real engines
md: The constraint and the prompt are separate channels. A mask can stop the model from writing an illegal token, but it cannot tell the model what the fields mean. If the model never sees the schema (as with llama.cpp's grammar option), describe the fields in the prompt, or the model is forced through a format it does not understand.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
md: Design for the miss: the parse cache sets the mean, the deadline and keyword fallback set the tail.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
md: Do not compare quality numbers across papers as if the setups matched. First-stage retrievers, candidate depth and datasets differ (RankGPT and PRP rerank BM25 top 100; FIRST reranks Contriever top 100). Re-measure on one pipeline.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris scores a window by how much it changes under shifts in every direction. Both eigenvalues of $M$ large means corner; that is what makes a point localizable in two dimensions.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: "No mutex in the code" does not make an algorithm lock-free. If one stalled thread can prevent all others from completing, it is blocking, even if it only uses atomic instructions. Michael and Scott call out published queues that are "lock-free but not non-blocking" for exactly this reason, and Vyukov says the same of their own bounded queue (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: Lock-free data structures are two problems: the CAS protocol that keeps the structure consistent, and the reclamation scheme that keeps removed nodes alive until no thread can still be reading them. Get both right, or use a library that has.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Why log at all, and why not log everything
md: The log you need is usually older than the moment you learn you need it. Decide what to collect and how long to keep it from the questions an investigation will ask, then pay for that deliberately.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Alert quality: precision, recall and the base-rate trap
md: Low precision does not just waste time; it trains people to ignore alerts. Target's alerts were real, but an alert stream that is usually wrong teaches analysts that the next one probably is too. Precision is a security property.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: With dynamic scaling the RoPE of every cached token changes when $s$ changes. The YaRN paper notes the correct implementation caches keys *before* applying RoPE; caching rotated keys silently mixes two different scalings.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
